catalog_quote: [p. 106] Kurripáku é uma língua de acento "pitch" em nível pós-lexical. Isso quer dizer que o sistema acentual primeiramente é caracterizado por regras métricas e no momento final da derivação recebe uma regra de atribuição de tom alto na sílaba acentuada. [p. 107] o acento não depende de tipos de elementos formando a estrutura silábica, ou seja, não se atribui acento de acordo com tipo de sílaba leve versus pesada como os exemplos (101 b, c, e) poderiam nos levar a supor. Os exemplos (101a, e, f) nos mostram que o acento não ocorre numa mesma posição na sílaba da palavra fonológica. Sua atribuição tem domínio morfológico. Em outras palavras, o domínio do acento é a raiz morfológica. [p. 110] Isso nos leva a supor que existem duas possibilidades acentuais: Uma lexicalmente atribuída na sílaba anterior à última, no domínio da raiz, sendo ordenada antes das regras de ditongação e alongame…

new_statements.quote: O acento recai, mais frequentemente, na penúltima sílaba, havendo também considerável número de exemplos de palavras com acento na antepenúltima e outros na sílaba que antecede a antepenúltima. Todavia, como mencionamos na introdução deste tópico, o acento não atua somente no nível silábico, mas no moraico também, assim no caso das sílabas longas tônicas, há ainda um segundo acento que recai sobre a mora, fazendo que haja sílabas tônicas de tom descendente e as sílabas tônicas de tom ascendente. [p. 189:] [...] as evidências indicam que se trate, portanto, de pitch accent o tipo do padrão acentual em Baniwa do Içana e em Kuripako.
new_statements.translation: Stress falls most frequently on the penultimate syllable, there being also a considerable number of examples of words with stress on the antepenultimate, and others on the syllable preceding the antepenultimate. However, as we mentioned in the introduction to this topic, stress does not operate only at the syllable level but at the moraic level too; thus in the case of stressed long syllables there is a further, second accent that falls on the mora, so that there are stressed syllables with falling tone and stressed syllables with rising tone. [p. 189:] ... the evidence thus indicates that the type of accentual pattern in Baniwa do Içana and in Kuripako is pitch accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One prominent (pitch-accented) syllable per phonological word, never the final syllable; most often the penultimate, but frequently the antepenultimate or earlier, so position is not surface-predictable. Ramirez 2001 (central dialect) derives the same distribution from a penultimate rule plus lexically extrametrical suffixes; Ortiz Ovalle 1998 (Colombian Kurripako) calls the accent 'free' with a first/second-syllable tendency and preference for heavy syllables. On accented long syllables a lexical rising vs falling (high) melody contrast is superimposed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary word stress is described. de Souza's 'segundo acento' is a moraic pitch contrast (rising vs falling) within the single accented long syllable, not a second stressed syllable. Ramirez 2001 explicitly limits his account to primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: de Souza p. 190: nouns whose first syllable has a long stressed vowel lose both stress and length when a possessive prefix is added (stress moves rightward, e.g. ['he.ma] 'tapir' vs [no.he.'ma.ni] 'my tapir'). Ramirez 2001 (central dialect): most onomatopoeias are unstressed; the adjectiviser -me is irregular in metricity; all other suffixes are regularly metrical or extrametrical. Ortiz Ovalle 1998: stress can fall on any syllable (minimal pairs kóɸe/koɸé, íʂati/iʂáti).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: the phonological word, which for de Souza includes possessive-prefix + dependent noun (['ne.ʐi] 'their son'); data are elicited citation forms from one Baniwa do Içana and one Kuripako consultant (Brazil, upper Içana / São Gabriel da Cachoeira). de Souza reports Valadares 1993 as urging phrase-level study of accent; none of the sources gives phrase-level rules.
new_statements.identity_note: de Souza 2012 treats Baniwa do Içana (bani1255) and Kuripako (curr1243) as two variants of one language ('Baniwa-Kuripako') and states the accent facts for both, using one Kuripako consultant from the Brazilian upper Içana (Ramirez's 'dialeto setentrional', the one 'dito curripaco'). Ramirez 2001's more explicit rule (penultimate with extrametrical suffixes) is stated only for the Central dialect (Huhúdeeni, Walipere-Dakenai etc.), i.e. Baniwa do Içana proper = bani1255, and is already held under bani1255. Ortiz Ovalle 1998 describes Colombian Kurripako of the Guainía (curr1243) and calls stress free with a first-syllable tendency. Granadillo's work is on the Ehe dialect of Venezuelan Kurripako (curr1243).

new_statements.quote: [p. 54] O acento manifesta-se através do tipo pitch-accent. [p. 107] Em outras palavras, o domínio do acento é a raiz morfológica. [p. 110] Isso nos leva a supor que existem duas possibilidades acentuais: Uma lexicalmente atribuída na sílaba anterior à última, no domínio da raiz, sendo ordenada antes das regras de ditongação e alongamento, como podemos observar nos exemplos (108). Outra possibilidade é a existência de formas não acentuadas subjacentes, sendo a atribuição acentual ordenada depois das regras de coalescência, como em (107). [p. 154] b) a culminância acentual paroxítona;
new_statements.translation: [p. 54] Accent is realised as pitch-accent. [p. 107] In other words, the domain of the accent is the morphological root. [p. 110] This leads us to suppose that there are two accentual possibilities: one lexically assigned to the syllable before the last, within the domain of the root, ordered before the diphthongisation and lengthening rules, as we can observe in examples (108). The other possibility is the existence of underlyingly unaccented forms, with accent assignment ordered after the coalescence rules, as in (107). [p. 154] b) paroxytone accentual culminativity;

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for curr1243 has an empty rule; the existing statement (de Souza 2012, 'lexical (unpredictable)': accent most often penultimate, many antepenultimate and pre-antepenultimate cases) is compatible with Valadares's surface facts (accent on any of the last four syllables, paroxytone the default). Valadares refines it with an analysis: a pitch accent system whose placement rule is penult-of-the-ROOT with extrametrical suffixes, not weight-sensitive, one prominence per word. She also documents word-final accent ([ku.ɻĩ́m] 'não', position 1), which de Souza's quoted sentence does not list. Identity: Valadares's speakers are Kumandáminanai and Ayáneni clan members from the upper…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One prominence per word, realised as a high pitch (P4: 'atribui-se um tom alto no momento final da derivação', p. 110; 'Kurripáku é uma língua de acento pitch em nível pós-lexical', p. 106). Placement is computed on the morphological root, not the phonological word: a right-to-left grid over the root puts the accent on the root's penultimate syllable (P2, p. 110), and suffixes lexically marked <> are extrametrical unless a further suffix follows (P3; 'não-exaustividade', pp. 112-113), so the surface accent can sit on any of the last four syllables of the word — 'A contar da última sílaba o acento pode ocorrer em posição 1, 2, 3 e 4' (p. 53), e.g. [ku.ɻĩ́m] 'não' (final), [ma.ká.ne] 'grande', [ɻiʷ.pá.ta.ka] 'ele corta', [ma.tʃi.ʲá.pa.ɻu.pe] 'boas, bonitas'. Accent is not weight-sensitive: 'o acento não depende de tipos de elementos formando a estrutura silábica, ou seja, não se atribui acento de acordo com tipo de sílaba leve versus pesada' (p. 107). Acoustically pitch is the constant cue; intensity may or may not coincide (Gráficos 1-2, pp. 54-55). Summary in the conclusions: 'a culminância acentual paroxítona' (p. 154).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the theory chapter states the language has 'uma única proeminência lingüística' with only one syllable per word receiving it (p. 29).
new_statements.exceptions: Some roots are underlyingly unaccented and receive accent only after coalescence (p. 110, ex. 107, e.g. [ɻí.nu.ka] 'ele vem' from [ɻi]+[anu]+[ka]); accent shifts when suffixes are concatenated because the extrametrical status of a marked suffix is cancelled by a following suffix (pp. 111-113, exx. 112-118); Portuguese loans are said to conform to the paroxytone pattern (p. 154).
new_statements.identity_note: Valadares 1993/94 describes the Kurripáku spoken by two speakers of the Kumandáminanai and Ayáneni clans in São Joaquim and Camanaus/Areal on the upper Rio Içana (Amazonas, Brazil), which she treats as variants of the Baniwa-Kurripáku complex distinct from the Walipéri-dákenei (Baniwa do Içana) speech that the current orthography follows (p. 153); this is Ramirez 2001's Northern dialect 'dito curripaco' = curr1243. Granadillo 2006 (not opened) concerns Kurripako of Venezuela. The existing de Souza 2012 statement covers both Baniwa do Içana and Kuripako with one Kuripako consultant.

readall_conflicts: they differ only in analysis (de Souza: lexical/unpredictable; Valadares: a pitch accent rule on the penultimate syllable of the morphological root with extrametrical suffixes, plus some underlyingly unaccented roots). Valadares additionally lists a word-final accent ([ku.ɻĩ́m] 'não'), which de Souza's sentence does not mention. that record is not from text I opened today and should be checked against its file before being weighed. Granadillo 2006 (Venezuelan Kurripako) could not be opened (not reachable by automated download twice; PuRe copy restricted), so it neither confirms nor contradicts.

sources.note: Sec. 4.6.2 'Acento e duração' pp. 185-191: stress is distinctive (though no syllable-level minimal pairs in his corpus); it falls most frequently on the penultimate, with a considerable number of antepenultimate and pre-antepenultimate words; on stressed long syllables a second, moraic accent gives contrastive rising vs falling tone; the system is characterised as pitch accent 'em Baniwa do Içana e em Kuripako' (p. 189); stress and length are independent (p. 188); initial long stressed vowels lose stress and length under possessive prefixation (p. 190).
